newsitem.title: ITALY: Rich leaders to stay away from food summit.
newsitem.headline: Rich leaders to stay away from food summit.

text.p: Leaders of many of the world's richest countries will be staying away next week when heads of state and government gather in Rome for a World Food Summit called to shine the spotlight on the fight to end hunger.
The five-day summit, overshadowed by the immediate threat of starvation and death facing one million war refugees in Zaire, is being staged by the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation.

FAO director general, Senegalese Jacques Diouf, has said some 100 of the world's leaders will take part in the meeting, which opens on Wednesday, but has so far withheld names citing security reasons.
"It will be the first time in history that so many (leaders) meet in one place to talk about food security," Diouf said.

Of the world's richest nations, the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised countries, none except host nation Italy appear to be sending their highest-profile leaders, according to government officials and diplomatic sources.

The United States, where President Bill Clinton has just been elected to a second term, will be represented by Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman. FAO officials had said privately that they hoped Vice President Al Gore would attend.
Canada and Germany are sending their agriculture ministers while Britain has named its overseas development minister to head London's delegation.
French President Jacques Chirac, a patron of the summit, had intended to come but has other commitments and is sending Prime Minister Alain Juppe in his place.
It was not immediately clear who would represent Japan. Russia, where President Boris Yeltsin has just had major heart surgery, is sending deputy prime minister Alexander Zaveryukha.
Diouf and other FAO officials have defended the meeting from criticism that the world is "summitted out" and that the gathering is ill-timed coming so soon after U.S. elections.
FAO had initially hoped to stage the summit in early 1996 but Italy told the Rome-based agency it had enough on its plate then with the country's European Union presidency stint.

The summit is seeking no hard cash from governments nor will the crisis in eastern Zaire be directly addressed, though the presence in Rome of many African leaders means it is likely to figure in talks on the margins.
Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale also suggested last week that the opportunity for so many international players to meet might yield more than the summit itself.
He told reporters that he hoped to have unofficial talks, including with Glickman, on creation of a world food reserve.

"It is not officially on the agenda. But part of what will happen in Rome, apart from the official agenda, is a great deal of corridor conversations, which on occasion can be more valuable than the official proceedings," Goodale said.

Preparatory talks have already brought agreement on the two summit texts, which contain a specific commitment to reduce the number of undernourished people in the world to half the present level of 840 million by no later than the year 2015.
British officials acknowledged at a news briefing in London last week that the summit could look like a talking shop given advance agreement on the texts and the lack of focus on Zaire.
